thread.title: Alibaba knew about Spectre and Meltdown before the USA government

author: Ramona Zimmerman
title: Alibaba knew about Spectre and Meltdown before the USA government
text:
Alibaba knew about Spectre and Meltdown before the USA government January 29 By Ramona Zimmerman 
Intel is not having that great of year thus far in the face of a slew of information about security flaws in it hardware coming out - and you can add another new report from The Wall Street Journal today, which suggests that Intel didn't immediately notify the US government of the issues, to that list. 
In initial disclosures about critical security flaws discovered in its processors, Intel Corp. notified a small group of customers, including Chinese technology companies, but left out the US government, according to people familiar with the matter and some of the companies involved. Lenovo said the information was protected by a non-disclosure agreement. 
Speaking with the Journal , experts are saying there's no evidence the information was misused in any way. The huge debate arose from the vulnerabilities that could have been severely exploited by ill hands. 
Jake Williams, head of Rendition Infosec and a former NSA employee said that it was a "near certainty" that the Chinese government knew about the security vulnerabilities in the Intel chips from Intel's correspondence with the Chinese firms. They allow attackers to access a vulnerable machine and extract valuable data. Apple Inc. (AAPL) Slashing iPhone X Production Amid Weak Demand Apple's total production target for the lower priced models (iPhone 8, 8 Plus, and 7) is expected to stay at 30M units. The LCD version is expected to come in the price range between $650 and $750 and feature a 6.1-inch display. 
A spokesperson for Intel told The Wall Street Journal that it wasn't able to tell everyone it planned to tell because The Register made the story public before the company meant to disclose it itself. The flaws, identified by the Google Project Zero team in June , were to be disclosed on the 9 of January, but were revealed early due to commits that were actively being made to the LInux kernel. 
The firms were ready relatively quickly as a result of the early warning. "In this case, news of the exploit was reported ahead of the industry coalition's intended public disclosure date at which point Intel immediately engaged the USA government and others", an Intel spokesperson told The Hill. 
The Meltdown and Spectre flaws have caused widespread panic - and rightly so, since they theoretically can affect anyone using a computer. It's still going on. The issue, as you might guess, is that the company didn't appear to have accounted for the cyberwarfare implications of who it notified first. Related:
